extracted.intended_audience: aspiring entrants to The New Yorker cartoon caption contest; humor writers and caption creators
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing successful captions for The New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest, emphasizing word choice, brevity, rhythm, and fit with the cartoon's visual details. Geared toward people submitting short-form humorous captions to a crowdsourced contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose your words carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: “The difference between the almost right word and the right word... is the difference between the lightning bug and the lightning.” Select the single best word(s) to make the caption as funny and precise as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author emphasizes that the 'right word' can change how funny a caption reads; examples include preferring 'window treatments' over 'drapes' or 'curtains' because the unexpected phrasing is funnier. The right word may be technically incorrect if it improves the joke's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider visual/contextual details of the cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account elements of the cartoon (including color, objects, and implied setting) when composing a caption; some details are essential to the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a Leo Cullum cartoon that appeared in red, imagining the red was 'essential to understanding' the winning caption. Always imagine and use relevant visual/contextual details to inform word choice and punch line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of language — eliminate unnecessary words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the shortest possible form that delivers the joke; remove every inessential word to sharpen impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting contest editors: 'The real challenge... is making [a] general funny idea work in the shortest possible form—using the economy of language and emphasis that’s necessary for a good cartoon.' Examples: removing 'up and' from 'you’ll be up and running' produced a significantly higher ranking. Advice: ruthlessly trim to improve clarity and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting and delivery matter beyond having a good idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A good joke idea is not enough; you must craft the wording and delivery so the joke reads as well as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes many people will think of the same idea; precise crafting (word order, phrasing, brevity) can distinguish your entry. Pay attention to emphasis and how the caption will read aloud/in voters' heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid predictable or common phrasing—uniqueness helps in crowdsourced voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of crowdsourcing dynamics and voter behavior, captions that are similar to a better-worded entry will be dismissed; unique, better-crafted phrasing increases chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains crowdsourcing effects: once voters see a really well-worded caption they dismiss similar, slightly inferior captions, which causes those captions to appear less often and receive fewer votes. Aim for unusual but fitting phrasing to avoid being grouped with commonplace submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the rule of three/four and build pattern/rhythm when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer captions are acceptable if every word is needed to establish a pattern or rhythm that makes the punch line land; apply the rule of three (or four) to build expectations before subverting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every great caption is short — some cartoons require longer setup to establish a pattern before an unexpected ending. When using this technique, ensure each word contributes to the rhythm and payoff; avoid padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical correctness can be sacrificed for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a technically incorrect term can be funnier and acceptable if it improves the joke's effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the winning caption 'That explains the signature on the floorboard' used 'floorboard' although an architect friend called it a 'baseboard.' The author notes you can 'get away with a word that is technically incorrect' if it fits the joke better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetics and sound matter but context trumps word-inherent funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comedians and writers emphasize sounds (e.g., hard 'k' sounds) as inherently funny, but the author argues sound matters only insofar as it fits the caption's context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Neil Simon and comedic examples (and parodies) about hard 'k' sounds being funny, but the author says he doesn't find words inherently funny — rather, certain words will be funnier in a given caption. Consider phonetics but prioritize contextual fit.
